(3/5) Good foundation, not bad, but still needs a lot of work to genuinely rival some of the big players and is already on track.

Key points for me:
1. Security and release information
There is still important release information that hasn't been disclosed. If the game launches with DRM, a kernel-level anti-cheat/driver, or ever announces plans to introduce one, I'd immediately refund it and drop it. Until the game's final approach to security and anti-cheat is clear, I can't recommend purchasing it.

2. Endless SSS vs Red Rift 
There is some experimentation in SSS Endless and SSS Endless is super fun! Can see a lot of potential for this and there's a lot of good stuff to say about it. Bravo, 4/5!

However there is very little experimentation in Red Rift. It feels like a complete slog to maintain streaks, picking dedicated units that are outright broken for specific Acts or bosses, and following a how-to-guide on what to play. 

Runs are easily butchered from small mistakes. Don't even considered tank/supp (+ramps) for act 1 as you'll just not have enough damage for the Challenge Rift. The hps % effect should be removed entirely from the Act 1 Challenge Rift entirely.

You should never be able to start a run without a single power-up. Sure, it's preventable but it's also pointless. If people want to test stuff for more than a few runs, let them without being disadvantaged for a leaderboard run. Turning Act 1 into a small grind is well, something.

The hourglass catch-up punishment can also make or break runs from Act 1. There's a small number of runs you would just abandon due to a lack of B-tier upgrades (and your choice in comp/champ scaling throughout a genuine strat run or test), Items or just in general an econ issue that shouldn't make or break runs when you're forced to take the Act 1 challenge rift in Red Rift.

I have also never encountered 2 of the same champs in a single shop selection. They're most likely unique. I would possibly like a preview of 1 shop refresh possibly on a once per act charge basis to counter hourglass Act 1 starvation from an early break, already deprived of resource, but you can't even find a B-tier upgrade. Low chances of this ever happening but more noticed through the learning curve.

Most of this is just patching, balancing and QA. 2/5.

3. Readability and information
The game needs better readability and more detailed information. When game speed ramps especially at Endless SSS, it can be easy to miss or fact check stuff without vlog. Could also help for theory testing, statistics and tooling.

Challenges should expand or give information when making critical decisions. This also ties into how predetermined the meta already feels. You'll skip the Act 1 Challenge reward almost always because Act 2 is simply that much more rewarding.

Overall
It's a good concept with a solid foundation. I'm starting to think the game modes are starting to click and perhaps the novelty is wearing off but I wouldn't recommend it yet until the security/anti-cheat approach and final pricing are known.

Would I buy it for £20? Probably. £30 or more? Most likely not.

This is a great auto battler/team manager, with some caveats.

I've put in about 12 hours into this demo, and with each run taking about 12-16 minutes, that means I've done a lot of runs with a lot of different character combinations and team comps. That said, some characters are functionally not good, in that their team synergy doesn't allow them to be effective in high level runs. Once you start getting to SSS ranked runs, team comp, item selection, and ability choices are all essential to pushing through to the final phases and getting solid performance in endless mode.

I hate to call her out specifically, but Zuri is a classic example of this problem. Many classes have the ability to multiclass/spec, and some innately have this built in. Zuri is one of those, with an innate spec of Tank and, wait for it, Assassin. Now in any game you've played, have you ever experienced a tank and assassin playstyle working in synergy? Of course you haven't, because they're on opposite ends of the spectrum. Guildrun is no exception to this, yet somehow they gave one of their tanks the ability to scale off of crit. It creates such a small window for success that any misstep can tank (pun intended) your run, because your tank has a complete lack of synergy with itself, let alone the team at large.

Because of this balance issue, characters who lean more into a single role actually end up allowing for more varied playstyles than those saddled with an unbalanced innate multiclass. In higher tier runs synergy is everything, and if your team is multiclassing in ways that don't align, you're going to have shorter runs.

I'm currently ranked #486 on the leaderboards. That doesn't mean I'm the best at this game by any means, but out of 14K all-time players, that puts me in the top 3%, so I'm speaking with some degree of knowledge here. So this is a message to the devs: you have an amazing game, with some real highlights worth celebrating, but I highly recommend rebalancing the characters that come with innate multiclass mechanics you can't switch out of. Right now they're not good, and that makes about a third of your roster less viable than the characters who have the option to spec into a multiclass or not.

Second caveat: I'm hoping for some kind of permanent progression attached to runs at launch. Beyond moving up in tiers, there's functionally no reason to keep playing beyond pushing up the leaderboard, and for a roguelike to launch without any permanent progression feels like a misstep. Permanent progression is what makes even the failed or bad-RNG runs worthwhile, and right now in this demo, they simply aren't. If you fail, that's it, you're back to starting a run all over again, hoping your RNG is better next time. It just feels bad.

Despite these two caveats, this game is still a strong recommendation, and I'm genuinely looking forward to seeing what it has to offer once it's further along in early access.

Fun concept for an auto battler, I enjoy raising heroes to greatness. Demo has issues, but it has potential.

Mechanics that need work:
-Hero upgrades: I don't like that upgrading your heroes is up to chance and rerolls at the shop, I feel like more often than not I'm just slotting high level units into my team instead of building a cohesive unit, which takes away from the intentionality of a playthrough. While that randomness may be intentional, i don't like it; i wish there was an option to buy unit upgrades as a choice of resource dedication.

-Starting hero choice: Similar to the above I'd like the starting hero choice to matter more. I'd like it if either that hero was guaranteed upgrades, was slightly buffed, or you were unable to remove them from the roster; it feels so arbitrary right now, and you are likely to drop them as soon as you buy some better heroes.

-The storm: I don't like the storm mechanic; if you're going to introduce a mechanic like "stall" then it feels insensible to punish people for playing the long game. Just start increasing % damage taken by all units in the case of longer fights, rather than introducing a mechanic that arbitrarily kills everything.

-Stall: I don't love the stall mechanic in general. While it represents scaling in battle, i find it kind of arbitrary given the amount of relics you can find that reduce stall counters. It either becomes a non-mechanic if you get those, or your character might just be boned if you dont. I would rather there be hero specific triggers for abilities rather than just stall, "X hero deal X frost each battle for this ability to become effective" type of thing. It would make units feel more individual and provide minigames in unit building

-I read below from someone else that they wished items dropped in battle; i think that's a cool idea. more options would be more fun IMO.

Rapid fire issues with balancing:

-Tanks feel largely ineffective in the early game and still not necessary in the "late game" demo. As the heaviest users of stall, most of them are punished by early game low power and storm damage. Vanguards and warriors with armor and relics and vamp feel just as effective
-All of my runs end with one giga damage dealer and the rest are just supporting. Even when trying to diversify damage, this seems to happen. 
-Active skills are generally better than passive area damage skills and auto-attack skills
-auto-attackers seem especially lackluster, and though they have a place in the early game, they fall off hard with the exceptions of Irina and Rip; to the point you'd rather replace them with literally any high level active skill user you can buy later on.
-Skills that generate shards in battle warp runs around them
-mana regen seems by far the most useful item stat to have on heroes with active skills, making late game team comp/itemization feel repetitive.
-Fiona, Yuuna, and Irina seem like the best units in the game by a LARGE margin right now

Some final thoughts on vibes:
-I wish each run's customization didn't all take place within the shop; rather than buying heroes, it would be cool if you met heroes by the roadside and had to decide whether to accept them for early game power in liu of different/better/more cohesive heroes down the road. That would make hero acquisition feel less arbitrary as well.
-I wish items dropped from battle so they felt like rewards for victory instead of just another button to make numbers go up.
-I wish hero choices didn't feel so arbitrary, I'd like to get attached to the particular way I'm building a set of heroes each run. Introducing some hero scarcity into game could be good here. 
-Some mechanics could be tweaked to make the actual battle more interesting and make each hero feel more unique.

Let me get this out of the way first: Solo Leveling is the modern epidemic of brainrot pop culture and one of the dumbest anime/manhwa I have ever sat through. So when a game shows up wearing that exact costume, rifts tearing open, guilds, heroes snowballing into absurd power spikes, my expectations were on the floor. The story and the whole setting are as generic as you'd fear.

Which makes it all the more surprising that the game is actually good.

The build freedom is the real draw. Bending heroes out of their starting class, stacking items and relics until something breaks in your favor, then pivoting mid-run when the shop hands you something you didn't plan for. It's the kind of loop where you say "one more run" and then it's 2am. No PvP meta breathing down your neck means you can chase stupid ideas and get rewarded for them. 

What I'd like to see improved:

- Battlefield layouts in the vein of Heroes of Might and Magic, or just more variety in the maps in general. Right now they blur together.
- Different map backgrounds and ground textures, purely for visual variety.
- Skins for heroes.
- More heroes.
- More environmental detail so the game feels a bit more alive and actually reads like a dungeon crawler instead of a board floating in space.
- More monster variety. 
- An item comparison tooltip: hold Shift (or something similar) and show exactly how an item changes the hero's stats and abilities before I commit. Right now there's more guesswork than there needs to be.

None of that is a dealbreaker. The core is strong and the devs are clearly patching and listening. If the presentation catches up to the systems, this goes from good to great.

TLDR; Worth your time and money.

review:
[h2]A superb PvE take on [i]Teamfight Tactics[/i][/h2]

I've spent thousands of hours playing [i]Teamfight Tactics[/i] and have hit Rank 1 Challenger, so I came into this with a pretty high bar for autobattlers. Thankfully, I think this game has a [i]lot[/i] going for it.

✅ [b][i]Gorgeous character designs, illustrations, and arenas[/i][/b]
The 2D character art is lovely, and each character feels distinct. Their designs also match their abilities really well. KT, the artist, is also super kind and clearly very passionate about the game based on my interactions with her in the Discord.

✅ [b][i]Lots of build variety and interesting mechanics[/i][/b]
There's a lot of cool stuff to choose from for each character, and the backup mechanic adds another interesting layer by letting you bring powerful effects from your bench into your deployed team. I also love how many opportunities there are to play greedy scaling builds while still having to balance them against "win now" relics, characters, abilities, and events, especially on the higher difficulties.

✅ [b][i]Fantastic UI/UX[/i][/b]
Everything is laid out really well, and I never found myself searching for anything. The compendium is also really well thought out.

⛔ [b][i]Endless mode needs a rework[/i][/b]
This is probably my biggest issue, mostly because endless is where I expect to spend most of my time. I think the game has a great foundation for endless, with characters, abilities, and some items that can scale. However, there's currently not enough to do once you enter endless mode. Upgrades become scarce, you can't spend your shards, and enemies start scaling so quickly that runs often end before I can really see how far I can push a character or team.

I'd love to see endless get its own progression system with more ways to keep developing your build, whether that's additional abilities, character upgrades beyond S rank, rarer items, or something else entirely. I'd also like to see difficulty increase in more interesting ways rather than just multiplying enemy health and damage. Slower enemy scaling would give weaker characters and more experimental builds a chance to go further.

⛔ [b][i]Shop system needs some work[/i][/b]
The limited number of shops makes finding copies of the characters you need surprisingly frustrating. Since character level also determines the number of item slots, entering endless without fully upgraded characters feels especially bad because you have no way to finish those upgrades afterward.

I'm also not a fan of shop rerolls getting more expensive after each reroll. It makes early-game rerolls feel overly punishing, while the limited number of shops due to not having them past Act 2 means you're often forced to reroll a lot when looking for key items or character upgrades. I do think this is tricky to balance, though, since shard generation is very accessible.

⛔ [b][i]Some backup abilities need a rework[/i][/b]
The backup system is really cool, but some of the abilities feel way too weak right now. Since you're giving up a character slot to use them, I think the weaker backup abilities need to provide a much more meaningful payoff.

⛔ [b][i]Some skills and archetypes need more attention[/i][/b]
There are a few skills and archetypes that could use some work, particularly some of the stall-focused characters. In endless, you can end up one-shotting enemies for several rounds, which means you're missing hundreds of potential stall triggers. It feels pretty bad when you're trying to build around the stall mechanic and the game effectively prevents you from triggering it because your team is too strong.

⛔ [b][i]Enemy design & variety[/i][/b]
Enemy variety is pretty lacking right now, and fights start to feel repetitive after a while. I'd like to see a wider variety of enemies and bosses to fight.

⛔ [b][i]Item design[/i][/b]
I like the items overall, but there aren't enough interesting chase items. A lot are essentially stat sticks, while only a handful feel particularly exciting. I'd love to see more unique effects or even an item-combination system to create more build possibilities.

⛔ [b][i]Enemy loot[/i][/b]
I'd like enemies to drop more than just shards or provide stats for on-kill effects. Having enemies with their own loot tables for items or materials could make individual fights feel more rewarding and make choosing between fights more interesting. [i]The Bazaar[/i] is a good example of this.

⛔ [b][i]Run length[/i][/b]
Assuming the current two-act structure is just because this is a beta, I'd like to see longer runs in the full game. More combats and events across 3-5 acts would give builds more time to develop.

[h2]Grade: B+[/h2]
Overall, this is a fantastic demo that highlights both the strengths of the game and where it still needs work. It's also nice getting weekly updates, so it's been cool seeing the game evolve without having to buy into an Early Access release. It's rare that I put this much time into a demo, let alone spend this much time thinking about it afterward.

There's already a ton to like here, and I'm really excited to see what the full game looks like with more characters, enemies, items, and content.

Definitely one to keep an eye on if you like autobattlers.

This is easily one of the most generous demos I’ve ever played. The core combat loop and build variety are so addictive that you could sink hundreds of hours into this slice alone, which speaks volumes about the incredible value the full release is going to offer.

That said, a few friction points stood out during runs:

Meta Progression Wall: The permanent meta-progression dries up abruptly after just a few runs. Expanding this track will make consecutive attempts feel much more rewarding. Hopefully it's a lot more fleshed out in the full game.

Late-Game Upgrades & Pivoting: Mid-to-late runs lack reliable avenues to rank up newer heroes. Needing to pivot your strategy or adding a new draft piece late often leaves you stuck with a C-Rank unit, which is an instant death sentence at higher difficulties/Endless. Some form of late-game rank catch-up would make adapting on the fly far more viable.

Support Stat Scaling (Crit Heals/Shields): Damage dealers have rich crit itemisation, but supports are strictly locked to flat Magic or HP/s. Letting heals and shields critically strike, even with a reduced modifier, would open up far more dynamic offensive-support hybrid builds.

The foundational design for a PvE roguelite autobattler is outstanding. If mid-run pivot flexibility and long-term progression tracks get tuned, the full game is going to be an absolute masterpiece. Thank you for giving us such a generous demo for free, can't wait to try the full game.

TLDR: A game in conflict with itself, all about PVE, but filled with mechanics right out of PVP. Another dota-autochess clone, which takes a spin on the genre by cutting PVP out entirely, yet it makes you deal with all the same bullsh*t as all the other autochess games, optimized for MMR based PVP progression instead of PVE fun.

YAPPING: You can make winstreaks happen don't get me wrong, but you have to follow very specific routes that have any consistency, instead of focusing on fun builds - and the devs even seem vehement on nerfing that consistency out, instead of increasing it for worse heroes and build - which makes 0 sense for a PVE game. Why make the player choose between doing well or doing something unique? It's NOT PVP, you can DO BOTH, but the devs somehow do not understand this basic concept and main strength of PVE roguelike games

The heroes are great looking, with many build options, but the PVE enemies and bosses are super basic, and feel tacked on at the last moment. This was probably intended to be a PVP game for 90% of it's dev time, but it took so long to get out into a beta that the autochess genre almost died before it arrived, and the pivot to PVE is a desperate try to make something out of the project. Which on paper IS a good idea, if the devs can stop treating it as a PVP-without-PVP game.

Overall Impression

This is a  surprisingly addictive roguelike auto-battler. Take the team fighting strategy from League of Legends and mix it with the RPG elements of Diablo and put everything into a roguelike auto-battler and you have Guildrun. The core of the gameplay is for those that enjoy theory crafting and developing builds in action RPG games. The premise is simple- select characters and purchase gear and relics and see how your team holds up against progressively tougher enemies. The simple setup and roguelike nature makes it easy to pick up but challenging to master. There are plenty of opportunities to experiment and test builds.  Altogether it’s a promising offering especially for those that enjoy theory crafting and designing builds and team compositions.

Target Audience

The core audience for this game are those that genuinely enjoy putting together builds. If you like experimenting and trying different compositions, testing ideas and analyzing how it all comes together this is a fun offering in the auto-battler genre.

Gameplay

The core gameplay is fascinating for a theory crafting fan. You start off by selecting one unit among a choice of three. You then encounter a battle and if successful you then visit a shop where you can purchase additional units, gear or relics (team wide buffs). The basic premise is simple and very easy to get into. As you progress you’ll be given additional choices for encounters and various scenarios where the outcome can impact the rewards you receive. For example, you may be given a challenge to have reduced stats but a much greater reward if you are successful in the encounter. Eventually you’ll make it to a boss, which usually presents a step up in terms of difficulty. If you are successful defeating the boss you’ll be given access to significant rewards. In endless mode, this cycle repeats until eventually you are defeated.

The team building and RPG mechanics are fun and interesting. Just like in a traditional action RPG units are defined by their class type and core ability. There are various classes but they generally fall into the trinity of tank, damage dealer and support. Altogether there are 7 core roles (warrior, vanguard, assassin, tank, mage, mystic, duelist) and units can potentially take on more than one role with upgrades. In addition, units are  tagged with roles as well as their core mechanics (for instance dealing poison, frost, burn, etc.). This makes it easy to identify potential team members to build upon a specific combat mechanic. The interplay between individual character upgrades, items and relics makes for builds that can be powerful, unique, and satisfying to theory craft.

Art & Design

The art design is a bright stylized modern fantasy aesthetic. 2D art is very reminiscent of graphic novels with fine outlines and a stylized painterly realism. In game art is a more simplified version of the 2 art with a strong emphasis on easily recognizable silhouettes with less detailed color gradients allowing units to appear more like animated cartoon characters. Altogether the 2D art really stands out as unique whereas the in-game 3D renderings make it appear as a derivate of other popular games, like League of Legends.

Challenges

There are a couple of challenges in the game. Most are minor but some are fundamental to the overall experience. First, the rougelike nature means that your run is highly variable. This is the nature of this style of game in this genre. Some runs you hit all the right characters, gear and relics and you dominate. While on other runs you may struggle to get past even regular encounters.

The more challenging component for this game is the difficulty spikes. In one fight your team may be doing exceptionally well and in the next encounter be completely decimated within seconds. The jarring spike in difficulty in some sections makes it challenging to learn how to actually progress. Complicating this factor is that there is a lot going on during combat with no real ability to implement any actual real time strategy, such as who your team should be prioritizing. In addition, the AI of the team and enemy units can make for awkward situations. Such as your DPS unit moving to the backline and getting surrounded.

Lastly, the main issue in the game is that although the auto battling components are fun and strategic, the nature of the game being an auto-battler makes the game feel repetitive and overall lacking a genuine objective. Once you understand how to build a team, it feels like a lot of how far you make it on a run comes down to RNG as you can’t necessarily progress into later stages without hitting certain survival buffs (ex. multiple massive shield or life recovery buffs).

The game mode that’s been presented so far (endless mode) seems like it is lacking something fundamental in its design. Although there are rewards for going farther, the goal to just make it one more fight and ultimately be defeated isn’t necessarily satisfying as enemy stats just get inflated with extremely high health and damage resistance. This makes most fights feel exactly the same. An endless mode in theory sounds like it could be entertaining since you can always push farther, but in practice it gets repetitive fairly quick.

In addition, there’s a lack of interesting meta-progression. Many roguelikes struggle in this aspect. Those that do this well usually have multiple systems in play giving players different ways to progress that allow the player creative choice and the ability to apply different strategies that are not all randomized or based on chance.

Closing Thoughts
Guildrun is a surprisingly fun auto-battler. There’s a lot of potential here. The actual team building and gear/relic combinations are interesting to explore and experiment with. However, the farther you get in the game the more that it can feel repetitive and that it may be lacking certain components in the design of it’s systems and core gameplay mode. There’s a lot to like in what is presented and with the right tweaks it could become a standout game in the genre.

The mechanics, items, builds and team comps are impressively varied and well thought out. Visually, though, everything feels a bit too miniature and could look more polished.

My biggest gripe is the combat targeting. Being able to choose which enemies your heroes attack, instead of steering everything through positioning, would make a huge difference. As it stands, the positioning system feels more annoying than fun. You can't reliably decide who fights whom, the enemy backline stays safe no matter what, and enemies more or less randomly teleport behind your own ranks. It's hard to see the point of careful setup when the game undercuts it that way.

The hero artwork is excellent, some of the best I've seen in the genre. On the battlefield, though, every unit looks tiny and underwhelming, heroes and enemies alike. The whole fight feels like it's happening in miniature. The battlefield itself could also use more visual interest, something like rivers, mountains, high ground or blockades to break up the space. Ability animations could be a lot easier to read too.

One more wish: I'd love to see the hero journey laid out on a map. Watching your party travel across an actual world would give the whole run a lot more character than an abstract sequence of fights.

That said, the game is a lot of fun and it pulls you in immediately. Build variety looks enormous. I can't judge the long-term appeal yet, but the potential is clearly there.

I love playing this game, but I unfortunately cannot recommend it in its current state. On the highest difficulty (Red Rift), there is a restriction that says if you have 10 deaths of any hero throughout the entire run, you immediately lose. In my opinion, this mechanic alone singlehandedly ruins the experience of the game at the highest level.

As you become more experienced at the game, you start to realize that the available winning strategies are very limited as a result of the hero death limit. Many strategies can be ignored entirely because they are an almost guaranteed loss due to the hero death limit. As a result, many runs start to blend together and feel very samey, and frankly boring.

I do not believe the game would be in a better state with the hero death limit simply removed, that would be too easy (same with any difficulty below Red Rift, once you have enough experience). However, the current implementation feels too restrictive. Yes, you can win very consistently even with the hero death limit, but the wins do not feel nearly as fun or rewarding because runs are too similar.

If you are familiar with Balatro strategy, it is similar to the Pair problem in that game. You can win very consistently in that game too, but when every other run has the same solution, it gets very old very quickly.

I think the game has a lot of potential, and was genuinely very fun for a while, but the hero death limit has been antithetical to my enjoyment lately, and any attempt at creating fun or unique runs will very often be shot down by an arbitrary death limit that says your win does not count. 

For example, Ming rush builds ("The Searing" ability), sacrifices almost all attempts at sustainability to apply as much burn as possible before dying. This could work great with the right builds, except for the fact that ming dying constantly will inevitably cost you the run due to the hero death limit. So instead, stack Rip HP, spam frost, instakill the final boss every run, whatever it takes to prevent deaths, because any strategy that risks any deaths is not a strategy you are allowed to use.

I cannot recommend this game in its current state because the gameplay loses most of its fun factor once you have enough experience and realize that the 10 hero death limit is the supreme ruler of what you are and aren't allowed to do in your runs.

What if TFT without all the nonsense associated with playing against other humans? Also add in the challenge of winstreaking at Spire-esque A20 difficulty? I'm sold. I am by no means a pro gamer, I've been playing for about 50 hours and I just managed to put up at 3 streak in Red Rift...but the feeling is incredible with that achievement alone. 

The game is fairly streamlined and smooth. The characters all feel different and (mostly) useful enough that you'll consider using most of them in the right situation in the right run. And knowing this is just the "demo" definitely makes me excited for what's to come.

The downsides? Some of the restrictions, limitations, and "challenges" of the RR mode do feel arbitrary and stupid. There are currently some options you will just NEVER pick. Period. And there are some things (the Rift Seal) that feel a little more annoying than challenging to juggle. But also I am still learning. You will also occasionally be offered "rewards" that are completely useless to your run. Three choices that are all either actively bad or irrelevant. But for a lot of these you get nothing for NOT choosing. In a deckbulilder (like STS) this is mitigated because not adding a card to your deck is actually usually a boon in disguise. Even a paltry 1 or 2 shards would feel better for passing on a bad set of relics. But this is a smallish nitpick.

My only other complaint is that the story is vapid and pointless. Having to smash through the even minor cutscenes is grating. The art style is also not to my taste, though I am sure there are fans out there. It's like worse Valorant. Yuck. But hey, I am still playing so whatever. I think the characters more or less look cool in game, for what that's worth.

Overall, if you like STS and TFT...you will probably like this game. The developers have the makings of a hit on their hands, but it will really depend what they do with it from here on out. I am really gun-shy because of crappy business practices recently in the industry (cough, The Bazaar, cough). Hopefully Leyline will make the right decisions where this is concerned. I recommend playing the demo as much as possible on the outside chance they botch the rollout of the final game.

I usually don’t review demos, and I don’t even like autobattlers, but this one really hooked me. I’ve sunk more hours into it than I have into many full-price games.

It’s a mix of Teamfight Tactics, Slay the Spire, and some really clever buildcrafting mechanics. It takes some time to grasp all the heroes, archetypes, stats, and synergies, but once it clicks, it feels incredibly satisfying. Since you have to rely on RNG (which heroes, items, and relics are available), every run feels different. At the same time, the reroll mechanics give you enough control to steer your team composition toward the build that best fits the resources you’ve gathered so far.

I’m really looking forward to the full release. At the moment, the only issue I have with the game is that at higher levels of play, certain relics seem almost mandatory. If you don’t find the ones your team composition needs before entering Endless Mode (and losing regular access to the shop after each round), you won’t make it very far.

I really wanted to like this game. I have been playing TFT since day 1, hitting at least diamond every set, and Ive also played a bunch of roguelikes, so this seemed like a slamdunk.

However, the difficulty (a big deal in a gameplay focused genre) is just a hot mess.

The game is laughably easy for the first few difficulty modes. I hadnt even fully understood the mechanics yet and I was still steamrolling every round just by all-inning on some trait or status effect. Then, somewhere around the S-Ranks, the game suddenly spikes in difficulty REALLY hard and I was struggeling a lot, but it was still okay-ish fun. The Red Gate however is simply a joke. I do not understand how you are supposed to make meaningful progress in this mode without giga highrolling. The mode also commits the same sin as Slay the Spire 1, which is to punish you on subsequent runs if you didnt get far enough on your last one. I understand the idea of the boss tokens, but in practice it just sucks since it makes your bad lack carry over from one mode into the next. They rightfully removed it in Slay the Spire 2.
Why would you limit items to one slot, then give the player a mandatory nerf item, meaning that you have to either nerf your upgraded hero or use up the one item slot on your C-tier to make them basically useless?
Why make the second round so hard that it cant be beaten by most upgraded B-tiers, forcing you to buy at least one unit in the first shop? 
Why limit deaths when there is a unit that revives others and there is a rewind that you can purposefully play around to get early ressources?
Only getting one loss makes it impossible to go for any risky plays, or to hold units in order to stay flexible since you have to heavily invest into your board every round in order to beat even normal enemies, meaning youre just rolling and praying to hit hero upgrades since they are such massive spikes. 

There is also no meaningful meta progression, and after around 10 hours I have basically seen all units, items etc and tried most of the combinations. I dont know how much more content is planned for the full release, but I lowkey feel like it would have to be an absurd amount like 2x to make this game worth playing for more than a couple of hours.

I am happy to be proven wrong, but this just feels like an half baked attempt of combining two super popular genres, there is no enough meat on the bone here.

I have played TFT for over five years and I think this game actually has great potential, although I think it still has a long way to go to feel more balanced and replayable.
 I really like the fact that all characters start at the same rank (C) and can be levelled up to rank S, but I think their evolution should be adjusted. The first upgrade characters get seems to be the most important. So levelling up a character to rank S does not feel as great as levelling it up to rank B. This is a little disappointing especially because we are not always able to upgrade all characters to rank S. So when we get the luck and gold to upgrade the character to rank S, it still is not as great as it should feel. I hope they can change it somehow or at least make it easier or less expensive to upgrade characters.
 I also feel that classes (like tank, mage and support) do not matter that much since you depend mostly on relics to boost the classes and the boosts do not seem to be that strong. So if you are lucky enough to get many heroes of the same class, it will not matter much. I think that should be adjusted. Otherwise people will only get the strongests characters every run. If classes mattered more, it would be more interesting to get weaker characters to fill the team up because of their classes. Maybe all classes could come with a passive skill that would get stronger the more characters of that class you have on board.
 It also drives me crazy the fact that you can only set 5 characters to the board, but that is better than having an unbalaced game. By the way there is one spot on the team that is only good if you're character has a passive skill that works from outside the board, so why not grant every character one of those passive skills at rank C already?
 I hope you are able to figure out how to scale character upgrades, relics and items well. Especially to make them feel that each has importance in their own way. Sometimes levelling up grants generic buffs that I think could be granted by relics, for example.

[h1]Le TFT solo qu'on attendait, dés capricieux inclus[/h1]
[i]On recrute une équipe, on redessine ses héros à sa sauce, on lance les dés... et parfois, ils ne veulent vraiment rien vous laisser.[/i]

[b]Guildrun[/b] est un rogue-like autobattler en JcE. On recrute des héros, on les positionne sur le plateau, on tabasse des vagues de monstres, on ramasse des objets qu'on équipe. Le jeu complet n'a pas encore de date, mais la demo est là depuis le 16 juillet. Pour l'instant, toutes les runs suivent la même structure : deux actes menant à un boss, puis un mode Endless. Seule la difficulté change.

[h2]Les +[/h2]
[list]
[*][b]✔️ Respec total :[/b] chaque héros a une classe et une capacité de départ fixes, mais au premier rang, il choisit une spécialisation parmi 3, qui peut carrément changer son rôle : un mage devient tank, un assassin repasse support. Sur 25 héros, la marge de manœuvre est réelle, mais elle dépend toujours du héros de départ.
[*][b]✔️ À votre rythme :[/b] pas de timer, pas de queue, pas de PvP à subir. On sauvegarde en plein run et on revient jouer quand on veut.
[*][b]✔️ Format généreux :[/b] certains joueurs ont déjà plus d'heures dedans que dans des jeux payants, alors que c'est juste une demo. Le coop, annoncé pour la sortie complète, promet d'ajouter encore une couche.
[/list]

[h2]Les –[/h2]
[list]
[*][b]❌ Shop radin, dés capricieux :[/b] le magasin ne montre que trois héros à la fois. On compose avec ce qu'on nous donne et pas toujours ce qu'on veut. Le reroll ne pardonne pas plus : on peut tourner un paquet de fois sans jamais tomber sur la pièce qui manque. Pour un jeu 100% JcE, sans personne en face à protéger, on s'attendrait presque à ce que les dés soient un peu plus pipés en notre faveur.
[*][b]❌ Peu de synergie cross-class :[/b] pour un autobattler à classes et spécialisations, les liens entre elles pèsent étonnamment peu. Pire : empiler des builds trop proches joue parfois contre soi, l'inverse de ce que le genre promet.
[*][b]❌ Sans plan B :[/b] deux morts et la run est terminée, aucune mécanique de comeback façon TFT. Shop radin et dés qui coopèrent rarement : une fois qu'une run part mal, difficile de la sauver.
[/list]

[h2]Conclusion[/h2]
Lancez les dés, mais n'oubliez pas qu'ici, personne ne vous jugera pour avoir abandonné une run perdue d'avance.

Very addictive gameplay. It constantly feeds the "what if I build my team like this instead"-feeling. Finding powerful combos of heroes and items feels very rewarding.

Only downside right now is the Endless mode. The demo currently has 2 acts, and after you finish act 2 you continue in Endless mode. Endless mode is quite boring because it becomes more passive, the shop disappears (which normally appears every wave) and currency and currency-based combos become less powerful. Instead you just get a choice of 3 things every 3rd wave. Hopefully they can expand the "endgame" and make it more interesting to continue playing.

There is no skill involved just RNG. During the honeymoon phase the game is great but it loses traction fast once you reach endgame. Since it prouds itself to be a roguelike instead of a roguelite there is no meaningful meta progression.

The scaling of the enemies leads to only cheese builds working past a certain threshold. Up until that floor you just steamroll the enemy and then your team dies in five seconds. You have to be extremely lucky to roll the currently viable cheese builds which will allow you to break through the magical scaling barrier. I'd argue that most of the leaderboard will end up at the same floor each week. 

Red Rift is a special offender for the restrictions it puts on your run. Most of the heroes in that mode are flat out useless. You can usually abort a run right after the initial selection or the first shop. Once heroes prove to work in that mode they will be nerfed on next reset. It's brilliant, really.

Since this game is essentially in development and the demo can be seen like early access for free, I will keep observing the development until it releases and change the review appropriately.

From time to time, I will check on the status of Guildrun and if it turns that I am wrong, them I will re-evaluate my review.

EDIT: I git gud. I no longer think the game is too reliant on RNG. Red Rift simply requires a different mentality and is an actual challenge mode rather than more of a "let's see how well your team does" kind of one. To beat Red Rift, you need to play the game, not fish for specific boards even though there is a fundamental team composition you usually adhere to. However, compared to endless modes going for high scores, there are actually more options as you do not have to just take scaling. Add that you are expected to keep buying and selling whatever you have, the game ends up putting the entire onus on your situation assessment and decision-making. So, I've actually come to enjoy Red Rift a lot.

The recommendation is no longer tentative.
EDIT OVER

This is kind of a feedback post and also a tentative recommendation because is the game good? Yes. Very much yes. However, on the latest two difficulties, the balance issues and RNG reliance become very transparent. If the full release will address these problems even just a little, it'll be amazing. Otherwise, currently, the endgame-ok builds are so limited that it feels more like a multiple-choice question than a sandbox. I'm certain the devs are aware of this, too, because the leaderboards for the last two difficulties are separate from the rest and each other.

If what they'll add in the full release is mostly just new items and new heroes, it'll just bloat the already large pools further and it'll make gunning for specific builds even harder, which is fine in terms of challenge but not so fine when it comes to fun, not to mention they have a trophy system for getting victory with each of the three specializations of every character. Pros
- The aesthetic and UI are gorgeous. It looks super pleasant, and the visual presentation alone made me fall in love with the game instantly. Plus, the clear visualization when passive skills trigger is a fantastic touch.
- Really cool character designs that grab your attention right away.
- Great skill synergies—when the pieces fall into place, pulling off combos feels fantastic.

Cons
- Way too much RNG. Right now, you can really only plan a build around your very first level-up choices, and after that, you're just rolling the dice.
- Crucial items and build-enabling skills drop completely at random, often too late in a run when your party setup is already locked in and you can't adapt.
- Missing basic safety nets like a skill tree or drafting controls to help target builds and cut down on pure luck.

Bottom Line:
Guildrun has a great foundation. When the RNG cooperates and you actually get to experience those skill synergies, it's super rewarding. I'm begging the devs to give us more ways to manage the randomness and let players steer their builds—let these strengths shine! Definitely worth checking out the demo.

An incredibly ambitious project that I can't tear my eyes away from. My only auto battler experience is really in Teamfight Tactics (TFT), and not even the PVP aspect. The amount of hours that I dumped into Tocker's Trials, the PVE mode of TFT is absurd. I play it on my tablet, when I'm bored on the PC, too much honestly. I play it until I understand every single possible composition and carry champion and build I can find. So much so that when I play PVP finally, I'm crushing the competition (in the beginning).

So I have experience in auto battler PVE, which is pretty much what this game is. And this game does that pretty damn well for its first bout. TFT had a lot of time to accomplish the shine that it has. This game is filthy by comparison. But it's not bad. It has excellent bones. I'll say shortly its strengths, then touch on its weaknesses.

Strengths:
+ Art style and design is fantastic. It definitely makes the genre its own with this art direction.
+ Characters are unique looking and cool. Essential.
+ Music is vibey and chill. Never really feel like turning it off.
+ Core gameplay mechanics mesh well together like Rush, Stall, Burn, Poison, etc.
+ Rank up system is unique and awesome

Weaknesses:
- Abilities seem very meh. I'm guessing this is just early stages but every attack, unless its big AOE, looks like a lot of nothing. It feels insignificant. And since most players are going to be playing at 3x speed (if you give players the option to speed up a pve roguelike autobattler, they inevitably will), every ability never stands out. Contrary to TFT where every ability is recognisable and standout thanks to its roots in LoL.
- Characters have no weight. Which doesn't make sense when you read it but let me explain. TFT and Dota's Autobattler has its roots in their original games, allowing them to take established characters that are already recognisable and just slotting them into their game. Making it easy for players to choose characters they already like or designs they like because they know them well and have seen them in action many times. Like how I play a lot of Riven, I will pick Riven a lot more in TFT. It creates attachments. Every character in Guildrun is working against this because they don't have that advantage, so they can't build attachment with the player. It makes every character feel like a statistic, just another pawn to use in this game of chess, rather than having a favourite piece or something you like because you like it. It's not helped that these characters aren't flashy (yet) due to the early nature of this game. The characters need more weight if players want to get attached to a repetitive game like this, at least to the same extent people are with other auto battlers like TFT in my opinion.
- The foundational gameplay is made up of a very small set of playstyles. Other live service autobattlers change up the way their game functions from the ground up every season, which reinvigorates the playerbase. For a standalone PVE only game, this is where I fear for the game, because I've already played a lot of builds. A lot of them. Burn. Ice. Duelists. Warriors. Mystic Shield Spam. Stall Spam. Rush Spam. Poison Hell. A lot of builds. Because of this, it feels like the game can hit a wall really fast because builds become repetitive quick. Tocker's Trials in TFT has the same weakness but it has significantly more diversity as well which stalls that out. This game doesn't feel as diverse because of its current state. Maybe they know about this and have ways to diversify the game, maybe have different guilds with 30 other characters and different base abilities. Kind of like having a different deck of cards. But Guildrun isn't like other roguelikes where you can just pick another character or deck to play, there's a lot more work that goes into making the individual "cards" function. The cards are characters that each need designs and powers. It's deeper, but not wider. And autobattlers can't be not wide. So I'm curious how they're going to attack this problem.

If this game is going to be a standalone indie game with no PVP, will it be a live service game that keeps updating? Having seasons that change how the gameplay operates fundamentally like TFT? If they don't, I have no idea how this autobattler is going to survive against free to play live service competition. Because as great as the game is, it feels like the game maxes out at 20 hours before I feel like I've explored every build and I get bored. I don't know. But I'll keep an eye on it because another PVE autobattler is something I always wanted so I can't complain about its existence. But I do worry for its future.

I wish there was a neutral review option. The game is initially very fun but it ends up feeling repetitive in a way other rogue-likes wouldn't. The balancing can feel quite bad at times because you either scale past the exponential curve in RR difficulty or you don't and there's no feeling of "hard fought satisfaction" like there is in other similar games. The challenges like the hero death limit can make gameplay feel tedious at times and there's definitely a "goldilocks zone" that can be hit between SSS and RR difficulty. However, that's something that can be addressed over time depending on the dev's vision. 

The main issue I have is with the game's aesthetic and feel. They borrowed ideas from Valorant/Hades but there's a distinct lack of charm within the artstyle that I can't quite put my finger on. Even in terms of gameplay, nothing really "pops" the way things would in other roguelikes would, (e.g a fat hit from Regent in STS or blasting a blind in Balatro), things kind of just flop over and die regardless of how you kill them. This is a lot harder but hopefully something changes for the better here. 

TLDR: Good ideas, fun initially but doesn't have the "sauce" :(

It’s not exactly a bad game. The problem is that the developers balance it not around the experience of the average player, but around sweaty, spreadsheet-wielding streamer min-maxers who play with a calculator open and casually vomit out 200-win streaks on the highest difficulty. As a result, the developers keep making the game more and more tedious (and I want to stress: tedious, not enjoyably challenging) to the point where it is essentially unplayable for normal people.

The Red Rift should be balanced around the median player: how often they win, where they lose, whether they understand why they lost, and whether they feel like starting another run. The proper goal isn’t “no one should be able to win consistently,” but “an average attentive player should be able to win, though never with complete certainty.”

And for the tryhards mentioned above, the developers could add a separate mode - say, enemies with 100x stats or a completely black screen. Something like that would definitely attract those guys, while normal people wouldn’t even seriously consider playing it.

Opinion of someone who has played a LOT of Hearthstone Battlegrounds and Teamfight Tactics:

I am 10 hours in and the higher difficulties are just unfun because the game lacks the elements of an auto battler that enable the same exciting tactics that an auto battler allows. For example, only having three hero options in shop (and the upgraded ones having abilities locked in) means I'm just praying that I can roll my character upgrades and I am NEVER pivoting build mid run because to do so would mean dying after two combats when my build fails to beat the scaled enemies. Whereas in a normal team battler I can afford a few losses while I search for the new units to pivot my comp. What this results in is repetitive gameplay that is just: lock in a team comp and pray. If I get lucky I get to advance if not try again. I do not think the Auction House is sufficient to compensate especially considering you need a relatively strong team to actually access it so why bother pivoting?
If this game wants to be marketed as an auto battler like TFT and others, you have to get rid of the "2 strike" rule where merely losing two battles will lose the run. You would instead allow for perhaps up to five losses or more for easier difficulties. The IMPORTANT thing is to allow for some pivoting (which also requires a shop rework...).

The first three fights at minimum need to be easily doable with any two-three characters at ANY difficulty. This is to allow for some exploration of character options instead of the aforementioned problem of being forced to lock in something with some synergy and never allowed to pivot.
Shop rerolls are too expensive (see above problem of success being too rng dependent and lack of pivoting).
The hero upgrade mechanism is alien to autobattler players and gacha players: Instead of using multiples of a unit to upgrade to the next tier, it just costs a ton more gold and is entirely at the mercy of RNG (because sometimes they get discounted ?!?!). Furthermore, am I crazy or are upgraded units in the shop extremely expensive even if I already have a version of them?

Grand Summary: This game was marketed as an auto battler roguelike but by stripping away many familiar elements of a real autobattler (cheap rerolls, multiple copies of relatively cheap units, actual trait synergy), the game is worse for it.
